feedback: If a child seizes on 'left' and subtracts 50 from 320 immediately, never forming the 4×50 sub-step: have them retell and represent the problem as ordered sub-problems on a strip diagram, and discuss why the cue word misleads here

When a keyword-driven wrong-order calculation lands far from the estimate and working backwards through the story (adding back all 200 pencils sold, e.g. 270 + 200 = 470, not 320) fails to return the starting number, point out the two mismatches and invite re-sequencing the steps
If the answer is 'more left than it started with' and the child is untroubled: require an estimate before computing and an inverse/alternative check after — do not reteach the arithmetic itself

If the child stalls and stops, model 'change course if necessary': show a second way to represent the same problem — for instance switching from a strip/bar diagram to a number line of the multi-step jumps — and name switching as a normal part of solving
activities.intendedInsight: Decomposition is something you physically arrange and sequence, not a rule triggered by a cue word; the estimate and a backwards check that undoes the problem's actions (not merely the child's own calculation) are two separate signals that can catch a wrong-order or wrong-operation answer.
learnerActions: Take a two-step problem, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' and arrange it as two connected sub-problem cards in the order you will solve them (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), adding more cards only if a longer problem needs them
Before computing, state 'about how big' the answer should be — set an estimate benchmark (e.g. 'about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left')
Solve each sub-step in order, keeping the whole plan visible

After you have an answer, work backwards through the story (inverse) to see whether you return to the starting number: put back the pencils that were sold, 120 + 4×50 = 120 + 200 = 320. Undo the actions in the problem, not just your own calculation, because undoing a wrong calculation (e.g. 320 − 50 = 270, then 270 + 50 = 320) would still get you back to 320
Compare your answer against your own estimate: if it is wildly off, treat that as a signal to recheck both the answer and the estimate
If an approach stalls, deliberately re-represent the problem a different way — for example switch between a strip/bar diagram and a number line that sequences the jumps — rather than stopping
activities.title: Estimate-first multi-step solver with inverse check

feedback: If a child picks an impossible answer, ask them to estimate first and compare against each option
For the runner item, if the child just multiplies, discuss what the situation implies about the real answer (more than 10× the 100 m time, not exactly it)
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation and attention to the real situation let you reject answers that cannot make sense, even before checking the full computation.
learnerActions: Given a problem and several candidate answers, decide 'which of these answers is impossible, and why?' using estimation
Examine two worked solutions and 'spot the wrong-order calculation' — identify where operations were applied in the wrong sequence

Reason about a realistic item: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — explain why it will be more than 10× the 100 m time (tiring over the longer distance), rather than multiplying blindly
activities.title: Reasonableness and wrong-order spotting items
